# Corner shop inventory

A small coffee shop sells three products: coffee beans (cost $6, price $10), mugs (cost $4, price $9) and paper filters (cost $1, price $3). The owner, an AI agent, decides every week how many units of each product to order from the supplier. Orders are paid for when placed and arrive at the start of the following week. The shop opens with $500 in cash and 10 units of each product. Each week customers want a random number of each product, and anything the shop cannot supply is a lost sale; unsold stock simply stays on the shelf. The owner can never spend more cash than the shop has. Customer demand must not depend on the owner's choices, so two ordering strategies can be compared on exactly the same weeks. Run it for twelve weeks.

## Deliverables

Report these outputs, using `beans`, `mugs` and `filters` as the keys of every per-product map:
- `cash_end` — cash at the end.
- `units_ordered` — per product, the total units ordered.
- `units_sold` — per product, the total units sold.
- `units_on_hand_end` — per product, the stock on the shelf at the end.
- `units_on_order_end` — per product, units ordered but not yet arrived at the end.
- `lost_sales` — per product, total units customers wanted but could not get.
- `demand_by_week` — per product, a list of the units customers wanted each week, in order.


Build this environment. Save it with write_contract and use the other tools as you see fit. Reply without calling a tool when you are done.

brief.situation: You own a small coffee shop. It starts with {$inputs.starting_cash|money} in cash and {$inputs.starting_stock} units of each product on the shelf. Every week you choose how many units of each product to order from the supplier. Orders are paid for in cash the moment you place them and arrive at the start of the following week.
brief.rules: Each week customers want a random number of each product. That demand is drawn independently of anything you do, so two ordering strategies face exactly the same weeks. You can only sell what is on the shelf: units customers want but cannot get are lost sales, and unsold stock simply stays on the shelf. You can never spend more cash than the shop has. The shelf view shows each product's unit cost, selling price, stock, units already on their way, and last week's demand, sales and lost sales. End the run with as much cash as you can.

roles.owner: Place this week's orders: up to three orders, one per product. Balance keeping enough stock against not tying up cash.

horizon.label: Weeks
horizon.description: How many weeks the shop trades.

target_stock.label: Baseline policy: stock up to (units)
target_stock.description: Target used by the built-in stock_up policy: order enough to bring stock plus units on order up to this level.

name.description: Product name; also the entity id.

weekly_demand.description: Units customers want for one product in one week.

cash_cents.description: Cash in the till, in cents.

stages.name: ordering
stages.brief: Week {$round} of {$inputs.horizon}. Place this week's orders, one per product at most.

order_stock.description: Order units of one product from the supplier. The unit cost is paid in cash now and the units arrive at the start of next week.

quantity.description: Units to order; limited by the cash on hand.

when.why: That order would cost more cash than the shop has.

order_stock.outcome: Ordered {$qty} of {$params.product.name} for {$qty * $params.product.cost_cents / 100|money}; arriving at the start of week {$arrive}.

till.show: Week {$round} of {$inputs.horizon}. Cash in the till: {$actor.cash_cents / 100|money}.

shelf.title: Products
shelf.show: {$it.name}: {$it.stock} on the shelf, {$it.on_order} arriving next week; costs {$it.cost_cents / 100|money}, sells for {$it.price_cents / 100|money}; last week customers wanted {$it.wanted}, you sold {$it.served}, lost {$it.missed}.

cash_end.description: Cash in the till at the end of the run, in dollars.

units_on_hand_end.description: Per product, units on the shelf at the end.

units_on_order_end.description: Per product, units ordered but not yet delivered at the end.

lost_sales.description: Per product, units customers wanted but could not get.

demand_by_week.description: Per product, units customers wanted each week, in order.

invariants.why: The shop can never spend more cash than it has.
Stock on the shelf can never go negative.
Cash is conserved: opening cash plus what customers paid.
Units are conserved: opening stock plus deliveries equals shelf stock plus sales.
Units on order are exactly the orders that have not arrived.
